comment:
So, the Maytag 10 year warranty is total BS!  After years of buying cheaper dishwashers which mostly performed well until the last one.  Because of that last one, I decided to buy a higher quality dishwasher with a stainless tub and a good warranty.  It was a Maytag with a 10 year warranty.  There were no cavoites as in it only covered the tub or the baskets,  it stated 10 year warranty open ended. Just under a year of purchase it wouldn't drain and me as the person that historically fixed everything, I was ecstatic that we could just call somebody instead of me coming home from my 12 hour day and putting in hours figuring it out and spending money on parts.  My wife called it in and in about a week someone showed up.  They told her that there was a $200 service charge which she wrote a check for. Without looking at anything, they then told her that it needed a pump and that the pump was not covered under warranty.  The pump was $120 and that he'd bring it in a day or two.  A week later he brought a pump and said he couldn't install it because the installation was below the floor and it had a hard line connected.  What it actually was setting on the subfloor a 1/4" under the linoleum. All that needed to be done was to; turn off the water, unhook the water line with a wrench, remove the two screws that connected to the counter tops and lower the washer wheels and roll it out.

Anyway his answer was he couldn't do it.  I got home that night, opened the box with the replacement pump and found the electrical connector broken and realized that it was pullout.  It was not new it was a part that had already bin inside of an appliance.  I thought this would help stop the money bleeding.  We told them we don't want it and we won't pay for it.  They said oh sorry but no we will send you another you've already charged and that's final.

I ultimately got down into it and found that there was piece of metal in there which I couldn't figure out how it got there.  In the end after looking online for photos of the replacement part, I finally found the original pump had a little metal piece that had broken off.  I removed it, and put it all back together.  It has worked well for the last 5 years.  I still have the $130 pump setting in my garage.  The 10 year warranty is total BS unless it blows your house up.

After all this I looked into the warranty system and found that Whirlpool had hired a warranty company that had previously been hired by several computer companies.  I'm so sorry I don't remember the company name but this company was being sued by many companies at the time because of how they handled the computer warranty claims.  I'm guessing that they decided there best option was to move to consumer products because computers are the life blood of industry and industry will pursure to the end of time but consumers don't have that gravitas.

Also I live in northern Indiana just below the Michigan border.  Just about 20 mile north is St Joseph, Michigan the original home of Whirlpool corporation where all of the engineering, design, and manufacturing used to take place. And just about the same distance to the west is LaPorte, Indiana where all of their service and training used to take place.  None of that happens in these places anymore.

We have had a series of Miele washers over many years.
They genuinely seem to design them to last for 20 years or more.

Our washing machines get a lot of use... much more than normal... and my sister insists on putting in too much washing powder or other detergents that cause over-sudsing (bad for the machine).

comment: The LG refrigerators suffer from a design flaw, the sealed system develops pitting due to the material used to manufacture the condenser lines, this causes a slow loss of refrigerant. The compressor has to work harder to make up for the loss of refrigerant, which shows up as your compressor running for longer and longer. This Speeds up the natural wear and tear over time and eventually after 3-5 years the compressor fails. LG was sued in a class action lawsuit twice, and lost twice, but they have not changed their design at all. Their resolution was to give people a limited parts warranty on the sealed system, first for a total of 5 years and then once they lost the second class action lawsuit, 10 years. This is why consumer reports gives them high ratings in reliability. Not because it is actually reliable, but because a warranty guarantees that the refrigerator will have a working sealed system for at least 10 years... but this comes with a caveat... you have to pay for the labor if you replace the sealed system, and you are looking at $300-$400 in labor costs for that replacement. Almost no one opts to do that.

comment:
What is rarely mention is
• the space that needs to be free around every equipment that has a compressor for cooling and/or heating and/or humidity control (laboratory climatic chambers). Nothing kills a compressor quicker than not enough circulation.
• a clean cooling grill or fins. Dirt build up, if not even areas blocked, puts additional strain onto the compressor.

My refrigerator is at a point to think about replacement. What I found is that the dimensions of the units are lying numbers. It isn't the physical dimensions one needs to work with but the dimensions given plus the extra free space. If there isn't enough air flow then the unit will fail earlier than expected, and what is more important, may not be able to maintain the temperatures.

I also know the same thing about electronics that can be repaired and those that can't, and those that use proprietary parts and those that don't, even a lot of very expensive electronics are made not to be repaired, and some might be repairable as long as the company keeps making their proprietary parts, they used in it, but most will stop making the parts 10 to 15 years out! comment:
I sold refrigerators, etc as a living. Our brand primarily was Frigidaire and related companies. White was bought out by Westinghouse. White-Westinghouse was bought out by the Electrolux company which also owns Frigidaire. I wanted a Samsung French Door, another brand we sold…got it and immediately regretted it. I really knew better as Frigidaire has far better insulation and really easy to replace gaskets. The refrigerator portion of the Samsung has almost NO insulation. When we lost power, it immediately got too warm…WTF? I was happy when the new owners of our house asked if they could buy the refrigerator too. 
Just remember the hierarchy of the appliances, White is what slum landlords put in cheesy apartments. Westinghouse is marginally better. Frigidaire is good and Electrolux is top of the line. But ALL of them , including other brands have components (all the lovely door electronics) made only in China. There were times when we literally had no water/ice through the door selections due to a shortage out of Asia. 
If you live in an area that is warm (southern states) pay the extra to get a “tropic” rated refrigerator. They are designed to handle the heat and are better insulated. You can see on the model number if it is “tropic” rated. (Your manufacturer will be able to list the meanings of all the letters and numbers…”tropic” is often listed as a “T” in the model number, but not always.)
While extremely prejudiced, our Electrolux supplier rep would refer to LG as “Low Grade” and Samsung as “Sam-dung” a bit of truth there at the time (10 years ago). 
I now live in the tropics on a Caribbean island and I swear by my 220 v LG tropic ranked refrigerator and my fantastic Samsung washer.

comment:
I have a similar model. The shelf isn't really made for mugs or anything bigger than a little teacup, HOWEVER it works great to wash flatware/silverware by poking it through the holes and letting it dangle there above the other dishes. You can get a lot of flatware up there, and then leave the bottom section open for actual dishes.

Also, since these countertop units rarely have a timed soap release door, they actually do better with detergent pods than with powder. They work fine with powder, but on the later cycles you won't have much soap left and they're working with mainly just hot water by that time. A pod will release soap a bit slower, so it's not washed out on the first cycle. Also, with these units (well, with any dishwasher) you want to be sure you fill it with warm or hot water, not cold. If you use cold, it takes a while in the first cycle for the water to get heated up enough to work effectively. It'll work WAY better with hot water in the reservoir or in the line, depending on how you've set it up.
